analysis.one_liner: Cuts power plant soot, smog, mercury, and carbon pollution by up to 90 percent.
analysis.headline: The Clean Smokestacks Act of 2005 was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to write rules cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide (the pollutants behind acid rain and smog) by 75 percent, mercury by 90 percent, and carbon dioxide back to 1990 levels by 2010. It would also have forced power plants more than 30 years old to finally meet modern pollution standards instead of operating under older, looser rules. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of coal-fired power plants — which is most of the eastern United States — gain the most: fewer asthma attacks, fewer premature deaths from fine-particle soot, less mercury contamination in fish, and less acid rain damaging lakes and forests. The bill also directs agencies to push energy efficiency and renewable energy, which lowers overall pollution and energy demand. People with respiratory illness, children, and anglers in mercury-affected waters benefit most directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents, children, and people with asthma

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA rules cutting power plant sulfur dioxide by 75 percent and nitrogen oxide by 75 percent from 1997 levels by January 1, 2010 — the pollutants that cause acid rain, smog, and fine-particle soot linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death.
Requires a 90 percent cut in mercury emissions from 1999 levels; mercury from power plants accumulates in fish and is especially dangerous to pregnant women and young children.
Requires power plant carbon dioxide emissions to return to 1990 levels, an early federal climate mandate for the electric sector.

Ends the grandfathering of outdated plants: any power plant more than 30 years old must meet the newest New Source Performance Standards and requirements for modified sources, closing a loophole that let old, dirty plants run indefinitely.

Directs EPA to coordinate with other agencies on energy efficiency, renewable energy, and cost-saving demand-side policies to minimize the economic cost of the cuts, and allows emissions trading for pollutants other than mercury.

Lets EPA require deeper cuts if the specified levels would not protect public health, and requires the rules to prevent localized pollution hot spots and ensure reductions in both eastern and western regions.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired and other fossil-fueled power plants pay first, through the cost of scrubbers, mercury controls, and carbon reductions, and those costs would be passed partly to electricity customers through rates. The burden falls hardest on utilities and coal-dependent regions whose plants would need the biggest upgrades, which is why the industry and allied members of Congress opposed mandatory multi-pollutant caps and backed weaker voluntary or trading-only alternatives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Power plant owners and their electricity customers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not say who bears the compliance cost, so part of the bill for scrubbers, carbon controls, and efficiency would likely be passed through to household and industrial electricity customers in the form of higher rates, with the sharpest increases in coal-dependent regions.

The 2010 deadlines for 75 to 90 percent cuts were aggressive; the bill allowed emissions trading for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, and carbon dioxide, and a poorly designed trading scheme could concentrate pollution near some communities rather than reducing it everywhere — a risk the bill tries to address by requiring prevention of localized adverse effects, but the remedy depended on EPA implementation.

Coal-reliant utilities warned that mandatory carbon caps plus forced retirement of grandfathered plants could strain grid reliability in regions dependent on old coal generation, an objection supporters would need to answer with transition timelines and reliability provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefits were large and well documented for pollution of this kind — fine particles, ozone, and mercury from power plants are among the largest industrial sources of preventable disease in the eastern U.S. — while the costs fell on a single, profitable industry and only partly on ratepayers, and the bill explicitly built in cost-minimization through efficiency and trading. The main honest objections are the electricity-rate impact and implementation risk, not the direction of the bill. On balance the design served ordinary people's health at the expense of a concentrated industry's operating costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Clean Smokestacks Act of 2005 on March 17, 2005, with 18 original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on March 22, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
That was the last action ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill had gathered 37 cosponsors — 27 Democrats and 10 Republicans — yet still never advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fueled power plant owners came out ahead: they avoided mandatory 75 to 90 percent emission cuts and the cost of upgrading or retiring decades-old plants, and electricity customers in coal-dependent regions avoided near-term rate increases. The public did not get the pollution reductions the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Power plant owners avoided the cleanup costs

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — 27 Democrats and 10 Republicans cosponsored it, with 10 Republicans among the 18 original sponsors — but the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans, so the split was less between the two parties than between the House committee's agenda and a bipartisan group of members.

industries.note: The bill would have forced utilities to cut sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon emissions by 75 to 90 percent and to upgrade or retire plants more than 30 years old that had long operated under older, weaker standards. Those are precisely the controls the industry would otherwise avoid funding, with the health savings going to the public instead.

A carbon cap returning power plant emissions to 1990 levels and forced modernization of old plants would have reduced demand for coal, the dominant fuel for the grandfathered plants the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency providers
industries.note: The bill required EPA to coordinate on increasing energy efficiency and renewable energy use and to include incentives for renewable energy in the rules, opening demand for those industries alongside lower pollution for the public.
Scrubbers, mercury capture systems, and monitoring equipment demand would rise as utilities complied, and the bill required that captured mercury not be rereleased into the environment.

Households and businesses would likely have faced some pass-through rate increases, but the bill aimed to minimize costs through efficiency and demand-side measures, and the health and environmental gains outweighed them for most people.
